newsitem.title: JAPAN: Battered Japan oil firms to cut capital spending.
newsitem.headline: Battered Japan oil firms to cut capital spending.

text.p: Japan's beleaguered oil industry plans to cut capital spending this year, and a deteriorating business environment means investment is likely to shrink even more next year, analysts say.
The industry has been struggling to survive on razor-thin profit margins since market deregulation in April 1996, which deprived it of its virtual monopoly in the oil product import business.
Excess refining facilities and petrol stations have also added to the oil companies' burdens, leaving very little room for the oil industry to make fresh capital investments, analysts say.
"The (industry) is over-equipped with facilities. There's no need for any more investments," said Toshinori Ito, senior analyst with Daiwa Institute of Research.
Ito noted that oil companies have in recent years tended to scale back spending over the course of the business year, thus spending less than levels set in their annual plans.

The most recent survey by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) showed that capital investment planned for fiscal 1997/98 by 37 companies in Japan's oil industry totalled 390.9 billion yen, down 17.3 percent from a year earlier.
"A difficult business environment forces the industry to cut investment," Ito said. "I expect capital investment to be even lower for the next fiscal year."

Investment in areas related to refinery facilities is due to tumble by 30.5 percent to 196.7 billion yen this fiscal year. A breakdown shows that large-scale investments in upgrading facilities meant to protect the environment, including desulphurisation units, will plunge by 73.8 percent.

Analysts said investments to upgrade units are now mostly complete, and the only substantial facility-related investments on the horizon are those to reduce benzene content in gasoline to under one percent by the end of 1999.
Takashi Kawai, analyst at Nikko Research Center, estimated that such investments would cost 10 to 20 billion yen for those companies that have not yet made the changes.
Japan's independent power producer (IPP) scheme, under which firms sell power to electric utilities, is about the only area where the oil industry might make significant investments, analysts said.
Nikko's Kawai estimated that oil companies would probably each spend 50 to 80 billion yen on IPP projects.
Self-service gasoline stations, which analysts expect will be legalised in Japan within the next few years, might also be a target for capital investment.

Most industry watchers, however, don't expect many such petrol stations to be built even after the ban is lifted. Japan now has roughly 60,000 stations, but analysts expect intense price wars to reduce that number to about 38,000 by 2005.
Daiwa's Ito said the most recent peak in investment by the industry was in fiscal 1992/93, when oil companies spent about 685.5 billion yen.

He said capital spending has spiralled downward since then, although the value of investments remains higher than in the early 1980s, after Iran's 1978 decision to halt exports and a subsequent oil crisis.
